transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-09
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Gupta (Redwood SE), Olivia Park (Redwood DevEx) - Jon Reyes (Starlit), Priya Nair (Starlit CTO), Diego Morales (Starlit DevOps), Ava Lin (Starlit FE)

Summary:
Quick SDK onboarding and Console/Optimize runthrough focused on auth patterns, local sandbox + CI secrets, and early performance configs (batching/cache). Agreed to share sandbox keys and a tailored batching config; customer to validate VPC egress and run bench prompts.

Topics covered: SDK install (py/ts), API keys vs SSO/SAML, local sandbox docker image, CI secrets handling, console routes and Optimize suggestions (batching profiles, prefix caching), Dedicated vs Hosted cost tradeoffs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for hopping on, we got about 50 minutes today, we'll walk through the SDK quickstart for Python and TS, do a quick Console tour and show some Optimize tips for your use case.
[00:27] Jon (Starlit): Yep thanks, we have a pretty small infra team so anything that doesn't need long on-boarding is great. Primarily interested in latency under 250ms P50 for chat-like prompts.
[00:40] Priya (Starlit): Also need to confirm data residency and KMS integration, we have to pass SOC 2 checklist for Q4 audit.
[00:51] Samir (Redwood SE): Totally, we'll cover KMS and the Private on-prem path briefly. For the quickstart, one of the patterns is to use API keys in sandbox then swap to SSO + short-lived tokens for production.
[01:15] Diego (Starlit): Quick question, the sandbox image you mentioned before - does it run locally with GPU or is it CPU-only emulation?
[01:25] Olivia (Redwood): Good callout, our dev image is CPU-first for fast spin-up, but we also provide a small GPU dev image for bench runs. It's docker-based so you can run locally or in CI. Link in the notes: https://redwood.ai/sandbox/dev-image (shared).
[01:48] Jon: ok, perfect. Walk us through the auth flow for the SDK then, especially for multi-env CI secrets.
[02:02] Samir: Sure, so for Python and TypeScript the SDK reads from REDWOOD_API_KEY env var by default. For local dev we recommend using the dev-keys we share, in CI you should use the secrets manager and rotate keys weekly. When you move to SSO, you exchange the SAML assertion at the control plane and get a short-lived token. Some customers call it a token swap.
[02:38] Priya: Will that work with our Okta setup? We need SCIM and role mapping, RBAC is a requirement.
[02:48] Maya: Yes Okta + SAML is supported, and we can map groups to Redwood roles for RBAC. We'll send the SSO integration guide after this.
[03:05] Ava (Starlit): Small nit - our frontend team uses TypeScript heavily, do you have examples for streaming responses in the TS client?
[03:15] Samir: Absolutely, we have a streaming example (ws & SSE) in the repo. Note that streaming implementation differs slightly between browsers and Node due to fetch vs websocket behavior. We'll paste the code snippet to the shared doc.
[03:42] Jon: About cost -- can you explain the Dedicated vs Hosted math? We might prefer Hosted to start but want predictable tail latency.
[03:51] Maya: Hosted is easiest to start, pay-per-use. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools, lower unit costs at scale, and capacity isolation. For a 1M token/month workload Dedicated typically saves ~30% depending on batching. But that depends heavily on token mix and sequence lengths.
[04:18] Priya: Any way to get quick sim data? We need to model our expected cost.
[04:25] Samir: We sent a benchmark workbook example earlier - we'll share a tailored sheet. For now, Optimize suggestions like prefix caching and continuous batching can improve cost by 20-40% on chat workloads.
[04:48] Diego: What's prefix caching again? I heard 'KV cache' in the docs but want a plain explainer.
[04:57] Samir: It's essentially keeping the key-value cache warm for repeated prefixes; reduces compute if you have many similar prompts. In our docs sometimes transcribed as 'kay vee cache' so apologies for the confusion in auto notes.
[05:18] Jon: Cool. Can you demo the quickstart flow?
[05:25] Maya: Yep, quick demo. I'm going to share my screen - starting at the repo, pip install redwood-sdk, set env var REDWOOD_API_KEY, run the example.
[05:39] (screen share noise)
[05:45] Maya: Here's the sample Python snippet - import redwood; client = redwood.Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); resp = client.generate('Summarize this bug report') - it's intentionally minimal.
[06:05] Jon: Looks straightforward, what's the default model?
[06:11] Samir: By default it points to our curated stable model in the catalog, you can override model param to a quantized variant for cost savings. The console shows recommended model profiles per workload.
[06:28] Priya: Where do we configure batching? We don't want batching to add latency for our interactive UI.
[06:35] Samir: Good question: batching in the runtime is workload-aware. In the Console/Optimize tab you can set latency SLOs so batching only kicks in within bounds. You can also set per-route policies for immediate responses. We'll demo the Optimize slider in a second.
[06:57] Ava: Any gotchas for Next.js and serverless?
[07:03] Olivia: Yes serverless cold starts change latency distribution; we recommend async streaming and smaller response windows, and consider a small warm pool or prewarm function. We'll add the Next.js specific note to the quickstart.
[07:21] Jon: Can we see the Console?
[07:26] Maya: Switching screens - Console -> Projects -> Starlit-playground (demo). On the left is routes, you can pin models, view token costs, and set rollouts.
[07:45] (murmur)
[07:50] Maya: In Optimize tab you can see inferred batching suggestions, and a recommended quantization profile. If you click 'preview' it simulates cost/latency tradeoffs.
[08:08] Diego: That preview - is it accurate? If it suggests a 40% cost reduction, should we trust it?
[08:14] Samir: It's an estimate based on your sample traces. It's good as a directional guide; we always recommend running 1-2 bench runs. The preview uses historical kernels and our workload model, but atypical prompts can diverge.
[08:32] Priya: About security: what audit logs are available? We need immutable logs for request metadata and admin actions.
[08:41] Olivia: We keep request-level logs with redaction options, admin audit trails for console actions, and you can ship logs to your SIEM via our webhook or direct S3 export. KMS integration for model keys is supported.
[08:58] Jon: Ok. Back to SDK: what about CI secrets? We use GitHub Actions.
[09:05] Samir: Use Actions secrets to store REDWOOD_API_KEY, and inject at job time. For higher security, use OIDC flighted integration so you don't store long-lived secrets and you mint short-lived tokens.
[09:20] Diego: Does Redwood support OIDC right now?
[09:23] Maya: Yes OIDC is generally available for GitHub and GitLab; we'll include the sample workflow.
[09:34] Jon: Any rate limits we should plan for?
[09:38] Samir: Hosted has tiered rate limits; Dedicated you can set quotas. Also we recommend client-side retry logic with exponential backoff; our SDK includes helpers.
[09:54] Priya: Let's talk about the private deployment option - we have air-gapped concerns for some data.
[09:59] Olivia: Private includes a customer-managed control plane and can run on your VPC or on-prem. For air-gapped we have an on-prem appliance photo but that one requires additional infra. We'll set up a follow-up to scope.
[10:20] (brief pause)
[10:29] Maya: Now I'll run a small local bench using the dev GPU image to show P50 numbers quickly. Running the bench script...
[10:45] (terminal noises)
[10:50] Maya: Ok sample run shows P50 ~ 210ms with batching optimized for short chat messages. That's using a quantized model variant.
[11:05] Jon: Nice. Could you export that to the workbook?
[11:09] Maya: Yep saving results to the sheet now and I'll share the link after.
[11:18] Diego: For our networking team - what egress ranges do you need for Hosted?
[11:24] Samir: We'll send a CIDR list for the regions you select; for peering we can also do VPC peering or PrivateLink.
[11:36] Priya: Is there any per-request metadata we can add for attribution? We need to tag requests with tenant IDs.
[11:44] Samir: Yes include x-redwood-tenant or metadata field in the request; Console will show breakdown by route or custom tag.
[11:56] Jon: On the SDK side: how do we handle retries and idempotency for generate calls?
[12:02] Olivia: We recommend idempotency keys for mutating ops and using the SDK's built-in retry wrapper for transient errors. For generation calls you can safely retry if you use idempotency to dedupe downstream processing.
[12:22] (crosstalk, short)
[12:28] Ava: Short question - do you guide on prompt design in Optimize? We have a lot of variability in prompt templates.
[12:34] Samir: Yes the Optimize product supports evals tethered to prompt sets; you can track quality regressions as you change quantization or model rolling. We'll include sample eval sets in the shared drive.
[12:51] Jon: Great. Can you walk us through mapping our route in Console? We want a /chat endpoint mapped.
[12:58] Maya: Sure - in Projects -> Routes -> Create route -> name /chat; you can pin a model, set concurrency and batching options, and add a fallback model. Also you can set per-route SLOs that feed into Optimize's batching heuristics.
[13:20] Priya: About fallbacks - if the primary model OOMs or degraded, what happens?
[13:25] Samir: Automatic fallback to a compatible variant, or to Hosted model in a different region depending on your policy. We'll show a canary rollout option too.
[13:38] Diego: Our most common prompt is multi-turn with lengthy context, how do you recommend using KV cache?
[13:44] Samir: Keep persistent KV cache for repeated session prefixes; use the console cache TTL controls. That reduces recomputation. Also note memory varies by model variant.
[14:02] (note: autoparsing sometimes labels 'kv' as 'kay vee' in transcripts)
[14:12] Jon: Ok we have about 20 minutes left - want to talk about a small POC scope?
[14:18] Maya: Sure, propose a 2-week POC: integrate SDK in staging, run 1k prompts, measure lat/units, validate SSO and secrets, and review results in a shared workbook. That should be enough to decide Dedicated vs Hosted.
[14:37] Priya: That sounds good. What would success criteria be?
[14:41] Maya: Key success: P50 under 250ms for interactive route, cost under $X per 1k tokens (we'll propose number), SSO + audit logs verified, and dev team able to run bench in CI.
[14:55] Diego: I like that. Will need Samir's help on batching config.
[15:00] Samir: I'll prototype a route config and a small docker image that includes the SDK and bench harness.
[15:12] Jon: Any blockers on our side?
[15:16] Priya: We'll confirm VPC peering constraints and Okta admin availability, and circle back on timing.
[15:24] Maya: Great. Quick recap of next steps: I'll send the sandbox access and the bench sheet; Samir drafts the config; Diego confirms network ranges; schedule the POC kickoff for next week.
[15:40] (wrap-up)
[15:45] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links and a calendar invite for the POC kickoff.
[15:52] Meeting ended.
